Grammar

will and going to (page 10)

going to: plans or decisions we made earlier.
I’m going to visit an art gallery this afternoon. I’m not going to go to town this weekend.
will: decisions or offers we make as we speak.
I’ll come with you! I won’t come with you. I’m too busy.
’ll = will   won’t = will not

Present continuous with future meaning (page 11)

Use it for definite future plans and arrangements.
We’re meeting at ten o’clock. I’m not doing anything. What are you doing today?

First conditional (page 18)

Things that might happen in the future.
If + present simple, will / won’t + verb
If the weather is good, we’ll go paragliding. If you don’t like it, I won’t take you again.
The two parts can swap places: I won’t take you again if you don’t like it.
Question: Will you come for a walk if the weather is good? Yes, I will. / No, I won’t.

Second conditional (page 19)

Things that are unreal or unlikely to happen in the future.
If + past simple, would / wouldn’t + verb
If I had a camera, I’d take a picture. If I had longer legs, I wouldn’t play so badly.
Question: Would you play rugby if you lived in England? Yes, I would. / No, I wouldn’t.
’d = would   wouldn’t = would not

Word building

un- / im- (page 9): popular → unpopular, friendly → unfriendly, tidy → untidy; patient → impatient, possible → impossible, polite → impolite
dis- / in- (page 17): honest → dishonest, like → dislike, obey → disobey; correct → incorrect, experienced → inexperienced, sensitive → insensitive
-ous (page 25): danger → dangerous, poison → poisonous, hazard → hazardous.
Noun ends in -e: remove the -e: fame → famous, adventure → adventurous.
Noun ends in -y: change -y to -i: fury → furious.

Writing a story (page 14)

  • Start a new line when someone new speaks.
  • Use adverbs to describe how people say things and how they feel (nervously).
  • When we know who is speaking, we do not have to put their name.
  • Put the speech and its punctuation inside the speech marks.
“What’s your name?” asked Jessica.

Reading facts

Island Adventure (page 12): Max is staying with his cousin Jeff by the sea. The boys go to a small island in Jeff’s brother’s boat. The boat is lost, they try to make a fire, and Jeff’s brother finds them.
Tanya Streeter (page 20): she grew up on Grand Cayman Island and loved the sea. Her sport is free-diving: people dive as deep as possible with no breathing equipment. At 25 she broke her first world record by diving 113 metres.

Paragraph writing Mine, not from the book

The teacher did not give model paragraphs, so these are examples I wrote to help you practise. Write 6–9 lines in your own words.

1. My summer
This summer I visited my grandparents in the village. I woke up early every morning and helped my grandfather in the garden. In the afternoons I played with my cousins and we swam in the river. We went to the market and I bought a new notebook. In the evenings we ate dinner together and told stories. I read three books and I learnt to ride a bike. It was the best summer ever, and next summer I’m going to visit them again.
Ideas: where you went, who you were with, what you did, what you ate, what you learnt, your favourite day, your plans for next summer.
2. The advantages / importance of teamwork
Teamwork is very important because people can do more together than alone. When we work in a team, we share the work, so it is easier and faster. We also share ideas, and good ideas make the project better. Teamwork helps us to learn from each other and to be patient and polite. If one person has a problem, the others can help. In a football team, for example, every player has a job, and the team wins when everyone helps. That is why teamwork is a good habit for school and life.
Ideas: share the work, share ideas, learn from each other, help each other, finish faster, example from school or sport.
